note.en: What you see: The arrest protocol fits the echo into the rhythm check pause without stretching it. The subxiphoid window shows one of three states: organised beating with a pulse meaning return of circulation, organised motion without a pulse meaning pulseless electrical activity, or a still heart meaning asystole. Around the heart the scan hunts reversible causes: tamponade fluid, a huge dilated right heart suggesting massive embolus, and empty flat chambers suggesting profound volume loss.

Common mistakes and correction: Stretching the pause to finish the scan: the clock owns the pause, so lift at 10 seconds regardless. Calling drifting clot echoes true motion: confirm organised wall contraction. Scanning without a preset so the heart never appears in time: set the subxiphoid preset before the pause arrives.

Normal values with units: Every pause lasts 10 seconds or less from stop to restart of compressions. Reversible causes to name on the scan are tamponade fluid, tension pneumothorax pattern where lung views are added, and profound hypovolaemia. No single finding alone decides when to stop resuscitation.

Pitfalls: The scan must never delay compressions, adrenaline, defibrillation or airway care. A poor window during transport is common, so state the limitation plainly. Debrief the clips after the event so the team learns without blame.

todo.en: How to get it step by step: Pre position the probe on the belly during compressions with the machine set to the subxiphoid preset. At the pause, place flat and aim at the left shoulder. Record a short clip and call the state in plain words. Hunt the reversible causes in the same clip: pericardial fluid, right heart size and chamber filling. Lift the probe and restart compressions at or before 10 seconds. Report the clip to the team leader after compressions resume.

remember.en: Hunt reversible causes without delaying care
